findings.issue_text: [BUG] The dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import and is a raw datetime that celery's JSON serializer cannot encode when `assignment_source.to_dict()` is passed as a task kwarg. The moment any inbound integration assignment flows through sync_group_assignee_inbound, GroupAssignee.objects.assign passes a non-None assignment_source, sync_group_assignee_outbound calls `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={... "assignment_source_dict": assignment_source.to_dict()})`, and the celery task fails to enqueue with "Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable" — the outbound assignee sync never runs, breaking assignee sync entirely for integrations that set assignment_source.

[BUG] The `queued` default `timezone.now()` is evaluated at class-definition time, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value shares a single immutable import-time timestamp. All sources constructed via `from_integration` report the time the worker process imported the module as their queue time, not the actual time the assignment was made; any audit/debugging or future staleness check based on `queued` is silently wrong.

[ADVISORY] The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter but no code path in this diff constructs or passes an AssignmentSource for status sync, so status cycles are not prevented. Users with bidirectional status sync between two integrations still hit resolve/unresolve loops; the parameter is dead on arrival until the status-sync call sites (e.g. sync_status_outbound callers and sync_status_inbound) are updated in a follow-up diff.

[ADVISORY] `from_dict` reconstructs `queued` as whatever type the dict carries, with no validation that it is a datetime, and the round-trip through celery JSON (if the datetime bug is fixed) yields a string. Consumers of a deserialized AssignmentSource get a `queued` field whose type silently changed from datetime to str, so any later datetime arithmetic or comparison on it raises TypeError at runtime far from the deserialization site.

[BUG] The abstract signature updated to accept assignment_source is sync_status_outbound, but the kwarg is actually passed to sync_assignee_outbound, whose abstract signature was not updated. src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py calls installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source); every integration implementation (VSTS, Jira, GitHub, etc., all outside this diff) still declares sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=...) without an assignment_source parameter, so the call raises TypeError and the sync task crashes for every provider the moment an assignment_source is present — and conversely sync_status_outbound implementations that faithfully copy the new abstract signature now accept a parameter no caller ever passes.

[BUG] The dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import, not per instantiation. Every AssignmentSource created after the first worker boot carries the worker's startup timestamp in `queued`, making the field useless for any staleness/replay logic and silently wrong in to_dict(); a correct implementation needs field(default_factory=timezone.now).

[BUG] sync_group_assignee_outbound puts assignment_source.to_dict() — containing a raw datetime under `queued` — into Celery task kwargs. Under the default JSON task serializer, Celery raises EncodeError (datetime is not JSON serializable) and the queued sync_assignee_outbound task never executes; even where serialization succeeds (pickle), from_dict stores an ISO string where the type annotation promises a datetime, so any future comparison on queued fails at runtime.

[ADVISORY] No test verifies that a non-matching assignment_source still allows outbound sync — the core claim in the comment "This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward" is untested. If the equality check in should_sync were accidentally inverted or broadened (e.g., comparing on provider name instead of integration_id), cross-integration propagation would silently die with a 200-OK no-op, and the test suite in this diff would stay green because only the matching-source suppression case is asserted.

[BUG] sync_group_assignee_outbound passes assignment_source.to_dict() containing a raw datetime ('queued') as a Celery task kwarg, which the JSON task serializer cannot encode. Whenever an assignment originates from an integration (sync_group_assignee_inbound → GroupAssignee.objects.assign with assignment_source), apply_async raises TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable, so the outbound assignee sync task is never enqueued and cross-system assignee propagation silently stops for every integration-sourced assignment — the exact flow this PR introduces.

[BUG] The 'queued' field uses timezone.now() as a dataclass default, which is evaluated once at module import time, so every AssignmentSource instance forever reports the server's import timestamp. Any consumer relying on 'queued' for staleness/dedup logic (the field exists specifically to record queueing time) gets a wrong, frozen timestamp; worse, the field is never read anywhere in this diff, making it dead payload that also triggers the datetime serialization failure in the Celery path — it should be deleted or computed in __post_init__.

[ADVISORY] from_dict returns None on any ValueError/TypeError (including unexpected/missing keys from schema drift), and callers treat None as 'no assignment source', silently disabling the sync-cycle guard. After any future field addition to AssignmentSource, in-flight queued task dicts produced by pre-deploy code fail to reconstruct, from_dict returns None, and should_sync's cycle check is bypassed — producing exactly the infinite assignee ping-pong loop between Sentry and the external system that this PR exists to prevent. A safer design would raise or log loudly on malformed input carrying an integration_id.

[ADVISORY] The diff widens sync_status_outbound's abstract signature with assignment_source but no call site anywhere passes it, and the inbound status path (sync_status_inbound / from_resolve_unresolve) never constructs an AssignmentSource — so status sync loops are entirely unguarded. The PR's stated goal is cross-system sync-cycle prevention, but only the assignee flow carries a source: an external issue resolved inbound resolves the Sentry group, which triggers outbound status sync back to the same integration with assignment_source=None, re-resolving the external issue and looping. The signature change is implementation work not traceable to any exercised requirement — either the status path needs the same source threading or the parameter should be removed until it is.

[BUG] AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a raw datetime and an int integration_id into Celery task kwargs, and from_dict() reconstructs with cls(**input_dict) with no type coercion, so after a JSON-serializing broker round-trip queued arrives as a string and integration_id arrives as a string, and the cycle-prevention check `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` in issues.py compares str vs int and always evaluates False, re-enabling the exact sync loop this diff was written to prevent. With a JSON broker (Celery's default), sync_assignee_outbound deserializes assignment_source_dict with integration_id="123"; should_sync('outbound_assignee', source) at issues.py:389 fails the equality check and proceeds to call sync_assignee_outbound on the same integration that originated the change, producing the cross-system assignment ping-pong loop the diff's comment says it prevents.

[BUG] from_dict() silently returns None on any malformed payload (including the datetime/type drift above), and sync_assignee_outbound then proceeds with parsed_assignment_source=None, so the cycle-prevention guard degrades to disabled instead of failing safe. Any payload that fails reconstruction (unexpected fields, wrong types from broker serialization, queued as a datetime object that a strict deserializer rejects) drops the assignment source entirely and the outbound sync fires back to the originating integration — the guard designed to stop sync loops turns off exactly when the data is imperfect, and nothing logs the drop.

[ADVISORY] The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition time, so every AssignmentSource built via from_integration (and every reconstructed-from-dict instance that omits queued) shares one frozen import-time timestamp rather than the per-enqueue time the field name promises. Anyone later using queued for loop-detection/staleness (its only plausible purpose, since nothing else in the diff reads it) gets a bogus constant timestamp; the field is also dead weight crossing the process boundary for no consumer, so either wire a real per-instance default via field(default_factory=timezone.now) or delete it.

[ADVISORY] Cycle prevention is implemented only on the assignee axis (sync_source only flows into should_sync for 'outbound_assignee' and sync_assignee_outbound), while the status axis (sync_status_outbound/sync_status_inbound) gained no source tracking, so a status-change sync cycle between two systems remains fully representable. Users who hit the assignee loop this diff fixes will still hit the identical loop on status (resolve in Jira → Sentry resolves → pushes resolve back), because the AssignmentSource plumbing stops at the assignee call sites; the design generalizes to status but the diff wires only one of the two axes.

[ADVISORY] The task passes assignment_source to installation.sync_assignee_outbound but the abstract signature in issues.py:411 declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, and every one of the many existing provider implementations (Jira, GitHub, GitLab, VSTS, etc.) overrides sync_assignee_outbound with the old positional shape, so the per-provider implementations never see the source — only should_sync consumes it, and any provider-specific cycle handling (e.g. Jira using the source to look up the external user) is impossible without touching every implementer. The next change that needs the assignment source inside a provider's sync_assignee_outbound body forces a coordinated signature change across ~10 provider classes; the diff also changes the interface contract while only IssueBasicIntegration's default and the test mock honor the new kwarg, so implementer drift is already latent.

[BUG] The `queued` field default is `timezone.now()` evaluated once at class-definition (import) time, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` gets the process-start timestamp instead of the actual queue time. Any consumer of `queued` for latency/staleness measurement reads a bogus timestamp frozen at worker import; the default silently lies about when the sync was enqueued.

[BUG] `assignment_source_dict` produced by `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` contains a raw `datetime` (`queued`), which the default JSON Celery serializer cannot encode, so `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` raises EncodeError when `assignment_source` is set. Every inbound-triggered outbound assignee sync (the exact path that sets assignment_source in sync.py) fails at enqueue with `kombu.exceptions.EncodeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable`, meaning the cycle-prevention feature never executes in production and the task never runs — the intended new behavior is dead on arrival.

[ADVISORY] `from_dict` silently returns None on any ValueError/TypeError, and the caller in sync_assignee_outbound then passes `sync_source=None` to `should_sync`, which disables the same-integration cycle guard. A malformed or schema-drifted payload (e.g. after a field rename, or integration_id arriving as a string during a rolling deploy) makes the cycle-prevention check silently vanish and the very sync loop this PR exists to prevent can re-emerge in production with no log line or error pointing at the cause.

[ADVISORY] The base `IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` accepts and ignores `sync_source`, and the cycle guard is only implemented in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`, so any integration or code path calling the base implementation gets the new parameter as a silent no-op. A future caller passing `sync_source` to an installation whose class only inherits IssueBasicIntegration gets no cycle suppression and no error — the guard's contract exists in the signature but not the behavior, and the next change to rely on it gets harder to reason about because the signature promises more than the base delivers.

[ADVISORY] The task passes `assignment_source` positionally/keyword to `sync_assignee_outbound` on the installation, but the abstract method signature change in mixins/issues.py only covers `sync_status_outbound` — `sync_assignee_outbound` in `IssueBasicIntegration` was not widened, so concrete implementations that don't accept the new kwarg raise TypeError. Any provider integration whose `sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=...)` was not updated to accept `assignment_source` crashes with TypeError whenever an inbound-sourced assignment propagates to it; the abstract `sync_status_outbound` gained the parameter but its assignee counterpart did not, leaving an inconsistent contract.

[ADVISORY] The new cycle-prevention behavior is only tested on the assign path; the symmetric deassign path added in GroupAssignee.objects.deassign (which now also forwards assignment_source to sync_group_assignee_outbound with assign=False) has no test that a matching source suppresses the outbound unassign. A regression where deassign drops or ignores assignment_source would re-open the sync cycle the diff claims to fix (inbound unassign → outbound unassign echo), and no test in the diff would fail; the existing test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign only asserts the assignment_source=None case.

[ADVISORY] The cycle-prevention logic is never tested in the positive direction: no test asserts that should_sync returns True (and sync_assignee_outbound IS called) when assignment_source comes from a different integration than the target integration. The new equality check `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` could be loosened to any-truthy-suppression (e.g. `if sync_source: return False`) and every test in the diff would still pass, silently disabling all cross-integration assignee propagation — the exact 'still allow other integrations to propagate' claim in the code comment is unverified.

[ADVISORY] No test exercises the to_dict → from_dict round trip that the Celery path actually performs, and test_to_dict's `assert result.get('queued') is not None` is a bare existence check that passes regardless of whether queued is a usable datetime. The round-trip the production code depends on (sync.py builds assignment_source.to_dict() as an apply_async kwarg, and the task reconstructs via from_dict) is never validated; a serialized payload where queued arrives as a string (or any JSON-serialization failure of the raw datetime in task kwargs) would pass all tests in the diff while failing or corrupting data in production.

[ADVISORY] test_from_dict_valid_data constructs from a dict lacking 'queued' and never checks the queued field, so the module-level `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` default — evaluated once at class-definition time, meaning all default-constructed instances share one frozen timestamp — is invisible to the test suite. Any consumer relying on queued to order or dedupe sync events gets the process-import timestamp for every AssignmentSource built via from_integration; the tests as written pass identically whether queued is per-instance now() or a shared constant, so the next change in this area ships with a false confidence signal about timestamp semantics.

[ADVISORY] test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration uses only mock_sync_assignee_outbound.assert_not_called(), a negative assertion that also passes if the outbound sync never fires for any reason (task not queued, feature flag off, config key mismatch), so it does not prove the cycle-prevention check specifically fired. If the new should_sync source check is removed entirely but the ExampleInstallation's should_sync is bypassed by an unrelated regression (e.g. org_integration lookup returning None), the test still passes, masking the regression; a positive control (same setup without assignment_source asserting the mock IS called) exists only for the None-source case in the other test, not for this integration's config.

[BUG] apply_async sends assignment_source_dict containing a raw datetime (from AssignmentSource.to_dict/asdict) in task kwargs, which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode. AssignmentSource.queued is a datetime; asdict() keeps it as a datetime object, so when the JSON-serialized Celery task is published, kombu's encoder raises "Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable" and sync_assignee_outbound never executes — every assignee sync with a non-None source is silently dropped, defeating the feature and breaking existing sync behavior on the inbound path (sync_group_assignee_inbound now always sets an assignment_source).

[BUG] Adding the new required-kwarg assignment_source_dict to the already-shipped sync_assignee_outbound task breaks coexistence of new producers with old workers during a rolling deploy. New-code web workers enqueue tasks with the extra assignment_source_dict kwarg; old worker processes still running the prior task signature (external_issue_id, user_id, assign) raise TypeError on invocation and the task fails/retries into oblivion, so assignee syncs enqueued during the deploy window are lost.

[BUG] The dataclass field default queued: datetime = timezone.now() is evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource created via from_integration (which never passes queued) shares the same import-time timestamp. The queued timestamp recorded on every assignment source is the process start time, not enqueue time, so any future logic or debugging that compares queued times gets wrong data; the field must use field(default_factory=timezone.now).

[ADVISORY] from_dict round-trips via asdict without converting the queued value back to a datetime, so any serialized/deserialized AssignmentSource carries queued as a string while the type annotation claims datetime. Consumers doing arithmetic or comparisons on parsed_source.queued hit type errors or silently wrong results after a JSON roundtrip; the try/except in from_dict does not catch this because constructing with a str for a datetime field succeeds at runtime.

[ADVISORY] The abstract sync_status_outbound signature now accepts assignment_source, but every third-party/in-tree integration implementation of this method that does not already declare **kwargs will raise TypeError once a caller passes the new kwarg. When a follow-up change starts forwarding assignment_source into sync_status_outbound, all implementations lacking the parameter (out-of-tree plugins and any provider not updated in this diff) crash with an unexpected-keyword-argument TypeError; the diff adds the parameter to the abstract base without updating the visible implementations.

[BUG] The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource instance forever reports the process-start timestamp instead of the actual queue time. Any consumer of `queued` (lag accounting, cycle-detection based on staleness) reads a fixed import-time value; after a long-lived worker has been up for days the timestamp is days old for freshly created sources, silently corrupting any time-based logic or debugging built on it.

[BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` embeds a raw `datetime` in the Celery `apply_async` kwargs (`queued` field via `asdict`), which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode, so the task fails to enqueue whenever an assignment_source is present. Once callers start passing a real AssignmentSource into sync_group_assignee_outbound (the whole point of this diff), apply_async raises a EncodeError (or silently drops the task depending on broker config), so the outbound assignee sync never executes — a user-visible sync that reports assignment success in Sentry but never reaches the external issue, with no task-side error since the task never runs.

[ADVISORY] from_dict returns None on ValueError/TypeError, which converts any malformed payload into 'no assignment source' rather than an error, disabling cycle prevention silently. If a producer ever emits a payload with an unexpected key or wrong type (e.g. queued as a string after a serializer round-trip), from_dict swallows it and returns None; should_sync then treats the sync as user-originated and the very sync-cycle this diff exists to prevent re-opens, with no log line recording the dropped payload.

The new tests cover (1) `assignment_source=None` still syncing (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign` asserts `assignment_source=None` passed through) and (2) matching-source suppression (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` asserts no outbound call). There is no test where `assignment_source` is provided but has a *different* `integration_id`, which would directly validate the comment’s intended cross-integration behavior and would catch an accidental inversion/broader comparison in `should_sync`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` embeds a raw `datetime` in the Celery `apply_async` kwargs (`queued` field via `asdict`), which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode, so the task fails to enqueue whenever an assignment_source is present. Once callers start passing a real AssignmentSource into sync_group_assignee_outbound (the whole point of this diff), apply_async raises a EncodeError (or silently drops the task depending on broker config), so the outbound assignee sync never executes — a user-visible sync that reports assignment success in Sentry but never reaches the external issue, with no task-side error since the task never runs.

adjudication.rationale: `AssignmentSource` defines `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` and `to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which will include a raw `datetime` object under the `queued` key. The diff then passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` directly into Celery `apply_async` kwargs as `assignment_source_dict` in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py). If the task serializer is JSON (common/default), a `datetime` is not JSON-serializable, so enqueueing the task can fail when `assignment_source` is provided (which this diff now does in inbound assignment/deassignment).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] from_dict returns None on ValueError/TypeError, which converts any malformed payload into 'no assignment source' rather than an error, disabling cycle prevention silently. If a producer ever emits a payload with an unexpected key or wrong type (e.g. queued as a string after a serializer round-trip), from_dict swallows it and returns None; should_sync then treats the sync as user-originated and the very sync-cycle this diff exists to prevent re-opens, with no log line recording the dropped payload.

adjudication.rationale: `AssignmentSource.from_dict` (new file) catches `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns `None`, and callers in `sync_assignee_outbound` then pass that `None` into `installation.should_sync(...)`. In `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`, the cycle-prevention check only runs when `sync_source` is non-`None`, so a parsing failure silently disables the cycle-prevention logic and reverts to legacy behavior. The diff also contains no logging/metrics for dropped/invalid payloads. However, this is only triggered by malformed/unexpected payloads, and the claim about `queued` becoming a string causing failure is not verifiable here (the dataclass constructor won’t type-enforce `datetime`), so it’s more of a robustness/observability concern than a guaranteed defect.
